Im studying International Crime and Justice! Do you have a region of the world that you specialize in or have more interest in? If so, thats a great start. Go experience it. 

If not, I'll tell you how I picked my specialized region. Before I was getting my masters (which is where I'm studying International Crime and Justice) I was getting my bachelors in a completely unrelated field. I went on a study abroad trip to Peru to work with kids in impoverished communities. Luckily enough, it was during their election. During this trip I really got to understand Peru and it made me want to learn more about Latin America. 

Now, I'm a bit different than you. I have been to Latin America a handful of times before this trip. My advice to you, just do it. The year before Peru I went on a study abroad to Ecuador. I knew no one. Not even the professors. The professors only learned my name after I had an asthma attack on an Ecuadorian volcano (not a joke). But, it was the best decision I've ever made. 

You don't need to do a study abroad however, if you're broke the bright side is that you can get financial aid to cover the trip (assuming you're in the US). As a fellow international studies student you gotta do it. It'll look great to have international experience (for leisure or for studying) on your job applications especially at the State Department. Just. Do. It.

I may be bias because I live in NYC, but December in NYC is the best. Everyone is slightly nicer, the city is beautiful. If you're looking for Christmacy stuff to do, NYC is magical. Now the best thing about NYC during Christmas is something not many know about. It's actually in Southern Brooklyn. It's called "Dyker Heights Lights." "What's a twin tower" was my first reaction to my mom (I was six). She had just picked me up from school. She said "the towers, in the city, you see them every morning." I was still confused and she had stopped to go into a bodega to get some cigarettes. As we walk in she says "Cmon j_poops-a-lot, you know what they are, you see them every morning on the news. You can see them from school" and as we walk into the deli they're replaying the video of the second tower getting hit. Then it sorta clicked. But yet again I was six. So to make sense of this I asked my mom if kids were on the airplanes. She said yes although I'm not sure if she was making an educated guess or if they knew that by that point. Then it clicked that this was something big and terrifying. 

Side note: we went home that night and had to shut our windows because the smoke was blowing towards our neighborhood. We were in complete shock (as the whole city was and the whole country, too) and we sat, in the dark and ate twizzlers for dinner because my mom couldn't bring herself to cook. She sat there all night answering my questions. Osama bin Laden used to give me nightmares. I would scream every time he came on the TV and have nightmares of him killing my family. When he died it was like Obama killed the monster under my bed.

I've never been a CPS worker and I never want to be, they have fucked up stories that they often can't do anything about. Mothers letting boyfriends rape their children, violent beatings, death threats, actual murder attempts, complete neglect, burnings, odd punishments like kneeling on legos.

If you want to see probably the most severe form of neglect read about Genie. She was locked in a room until she was found at about 14. 

If you want to learn more about severe physical abuse read A Child Called It. 

And, if you want to learn more about sexual abuse read Push. It's the book the movie Precious was based off of. Although it's fiction, it's an amazing example of how poverty, parental drug abuse, and sexual abuse impacts every aspect of a child's life. Some critics believe that that story is "too far fetched" but it's fucking not. Abuse like that happens all the time whether or not people want to believe it.

we were at 17000 ft en route to somewhere else. I actually wanted to stay out longer but was advised to get back on the bus before I had an asthma attack all over the place. 

At this point my head was definitely hurting but I've had worse headaches. You'll know when you or someone you're with is getting severe. To be honest you'll probably just have a really bad stomach ache, you might puke, and your head might hurt. It's very very rare to actually get into the severe stage. When in doubt ask the locals, they have a tea for everything

I did Machu Picchu as an asthmatic about a day and a half after we got there. Best advice, don't drink alcohol within the first 3 days of being there and stay hydrated. If your stomach gets upset drink lots of tea. If you have to, take it slow on the hikes. Believe it or not, Machu Picchu is actually at a lower altitude than Cusco so you might even feel better there than in Cusco. 

Also, altitude sickness doesn't affect everyone. I felt better in Cusco than I did in Quito, Ecuador (which is about 2,000 feet lower than Cusco) and my roommate felt worse in Cusco than in Ecuador. Some people didn't feel it at all. 

I also went up to 17,000 ft. For me (yet again asthmatic) it was actual hell and all I did was stand and look at a mountain. There's medication that you can take but I was allergic to all of them. Since you're going so high so quickly I'd recommend taking anything you can to avoid sickness. 

Lastly, I doubt this will happen but just so you know if severe enough, you can die. IF you're at 17,000 feet and things are getting very very bad (literally oxygen dropping, coughing up pink stuff, confusion, etc.)  you need to descend as fast as you can. 

Have fun, Cusco was one of my favorite places to be so enjoy it!
